projects.title: ESP32 Data Logger & Telematics Platform

case_study.problem: Commercial telematics cost ~₹50,000 per machine in the first year and locked CAN data behind a vendor platform. Internal dev and validation teams needed unrestricted access to raw CAN traffic without recurring platform fees.
outcomes: Reduced hardware BOM from ~₹50,000 to ~₹3,700 (90%+ reduction)
Annual operational cost ~₹1,000/device (data SIM only) vs ~₹5,000+/yr commercial
In-house ownership of all telematics data — no vendor lock-in
Continuous CAN/J1939 logging with daily folder organization
Live fleet map with online/offline device health
J1939 DM1/SPN/FMI fault decoding for diagnostic workflows
CSV/Excel/TRC log downloads for engineering analysis
case_study.architecture: Machine CAN/J1939 traffic is acquired by an ESP32-S3, buffered to MicroSD for local retention, and selectively streamed over 4G/LTE via MQTT. A Flask backend ingests the data, manages devices and users, and exposes REST + WebSocket endpoints. A Leaflet-based web dashboard shows live machine status, location and historical logs.
future_roadmap: Dedicated mobile app for field service
Hybrid connectivity: remote MQTT mode + local BLE service mode
Direct BLE retrieval of J1939 DM1 fault codes

projects.github_blurb: This project was built on private infrastructure at Ammann India. Browse my GitHub profile for other embedded systems work, schematics, and ESP32 / CAN-J1939 / IoT examples.
projects.short_summary: In-house ESP32-S3 based data logger + cloud telematics platform for Ammann Paver and Compactor machines. CAN/J1939, 4G/LTE, MQTT, Flask, Leaflet dashboard. Replaced a ₹50,000 commercial telematics system with a ₹3,700 in-house build.
projects.full_description:
Designed and delivered a low-cost, in-house Data Logger and Telematics Platform for Ammann Paver and Compactor construction machinery. The system replaces a commercial telematics solution that cost ~₹50,000 per device in the first year, with an in-house build at ~₹3,700 hardware BOM and ₹1,000/yr SIM — saving ~₹45,300 per device per year (over 90% capital-cost reduction).

The platform is a complete end-to-end stack: ESP32-S3 embedded firmware on the machine, CAN/J1939 data acquisition, SIM7600 4G/LTE connectivity, MicroSD local storage, MQTT-based live telemetry, a Python Flask backend with JWT auth, SQLAlchemy-managed data, and a Leaflet-powered web dashboard for live fleet map + historical log analysis.

My contribution covered the embedded data-logger architecture (ESP32-S3 + CAN transceiver + 4G + MicroSD), the CAN/J1939 acquisition and J1939 DM1 diagnostic parsing, the local log retention strategy, the 4G/LTE telemetry path with auto-reconnect, and the cloud backend / dashboard integration as documented in the project.

The platform supports engineering-grade analysis: raw CAN traffic retention, organized daily logs, CSV/Excel/TRC download, J1939 fault decoding (DM1, SPN, FMI), and a live map of every connected machine.

projects.title: Remote-Controlled Multipurpose Robot

case_study.problem: Build a wirelessly controlled mobile robot capable of both locomotion and basic manipulation tasks, demonstrating embedded wireless communication, motor control, and robotic system integration.
outcomes: End-to-end wireless control of a mobile robotic platform with a robotic arm
Real-time motor control with differential-drive mixing
Servo-based robotic arm control integrated with motion
Hands-on demonstration of embedded wireless communication, motor control, and system-level integration
case_study.architecture: A handheld remote controller sends serialized Command structs (throttle, steer, arm) over the nRF24L01 RF link. The robot-side controller receives the command, applies differential-drive mixing to compute left/right motor speeds, and drives the robotic arm servo accordingly. The system runs on two Arduino-class microcontrollers.

projects.github_blurb: This was an academic project — full source code and schematics are available on my GitHub profile.
projects.short_summary: nRF24L01 wireless robotic platform with an integrated robotic arm. Built at Government Engineering College, Gandhinagar. Demonstrates embedded wireless communication, motor control, and robotic-system integration.
projects.full_description:
Developed a remote-controlled multipurpose robotic platform using an nRF24L01 RF communication module for wireless control. The robot incorporated a robotic arm to extend the system beyond basic mobile-robot movement and support manipulation-oriented functionality.

The system is split into two parts: a handheld remote controller, and the robot itself with a motor drive subsystem and a robotic arm mechanism. Commands are sent over the nRF24L01 RF link, decoded by the robot-side controller, and applied to the drive motors and arm servos. The result is a wirelessly controlled, multi-purpose robotic platform that can move, turn, and manipulate objects via the arm.

The project was a hands-on demonstration of embedded wireless communication, motor control, hardware interfacing, and end-to-end system integration — the same skill set that translates to machine-control firmware and CAN-based actuators in industrial embedded roles.

projects.title: Smart Garbage Monitoring System

case_study.problem: Garbage bins overflow because collection crews don't know when they're full. Manual inspection is wasteful, and people often have to touch a dirty lid. Design a system that automates bin access and notifies the collector when the bin is full.
outcomes: Touch-free automatic door opening on person approach
GSM-based notification to the garbage collector when the bin is full
Door stays open during collection, closes once done
case_study.architecture: An Arduino Uno reads an IR sensor (person presence) and an ultrasonic distance sensor (fill level). On IR detect, the controller drives a servo motor to open the bin door; when the measured distance drops below a threshold, it sends an SMS to the collector's phone via the GSM module using AT commands.

projects.github_blurb: This was an academic project — full source code and schematics are available on my GitHub profile.
projects.short_summary: Arduino Uno based smart bin with ultrasonic fill-level sensing, IR person detection, automatic servo door, and GSM notifications to the garbage collector. Diploma project at Government Polytechnic, Ahmedabad.
projects.full_description:
Developed a smart garbage-bin monitoring and access-control system using Arduino Uno, ultrasonic sensing, GSM communication, IR sensing, and a servo motor. The system was designed to automate bin access, monitor garbage level, and notify the garbage collector when the bin became full.

Operation is two-part. The IR sensor detects when a person approaches the bin, and the Arduino commands a servo motor to automatically open the door — a touch-free interaction. In parallel, the ultrasonic sensor continuously measures the garbage level inside the bin. When the level crosses a defined full threshold, the GSM module sends an SMS notification to the garbage collector, who can then come empty the bin. Per the project logic, the door remains open while the collector is emptying the bin and closes once collection is complete.

The project is a clean demonstration of sensor fusion on a small embedded controller: ultrasonic ranging for fill-level, IR sensing for presence, servo actuation for the door, and GSM for outbound notification.

blogs.title: Embedded Fault Handling: From Detection to Safe Recovery
blogs.content:
A Fault Is More Than an Error Condition

In embedded systems, detecting a fault is only the beginning.

A sensor can produce an invalid value, a communication message can disappear, or an expected signal can remain outside its valid range. The software may detect the problem correctly, but the real engineering challenge is what happens next.

Does the system enter an appropriate safe state? Does the affected function react correctly? Is the fault communicated to other controllers? Is diagnostic information recorded? And when the problem disappears, does the system recover safely?

This is why fault handling should be treated as a complete system behavior rather than a single if condition.

1. Start With the Sensor or Input

Consider a system receiving a sensor value.

if (sensor_value > SENSOR_LIMIT)
{
    fault_active = true;
}

This looks simple, but several questions immediately follow:

  • What is the valid operating range?
  • What happens at the minimum and maximum limits?
  • What happens when the signal suddenly jumps?
  • How is a disconnected or invalid sensor detected?
  • How long must the abnormal condition exist before it becomes a fault?

These requirements determine how the fault-detection logic should behave.

2. Validate the Signal Before Trusting It

Not every abnormal reading should immediately become a system fault.

Depending on the application, signal processing may include:

  • Range checks
  • Plausibility checks
  • Filtering
  • Debouncing
  • Timeout detection
  • Signal-quality monitoring

For example, a single unexpected sample may be noise, while the same abnormal value repeated for several cycles may indicate a genuine problem.

This distinction becomes especially important in machines operating in environments with vibration, dust, temperature changes and other real-world disturbances.

3. Detecting a Fault Is Only One Step

Once the input is considered invalid, the software needs to decide what the machine should do.

A simple fault flow can look like this:

Normal
   ↓
Fault Detected
   ↓
Fault Active
   ↓
Safe / Degraded Operation
   ↓
Recovery Check
   ↓
Normal

The exact behavior depends on the system requirements, but the important concept is that the fault has a lifecycle.

It is not necessarily just:

FAULT = TRUE;

A robust implementation defines what happens before, during and after the fault.

4. Safe Fallback Behavior Matters

When a fault is detected, the system may need to limit a function, use a defined fallback value, stop a particular operation, or transition into another operating state.

The correct behavior must come from the system requirements.

The important testing question is:

What should the machine do when the expected input can no longer be trusted?

This question moves the discussion from simply detecting an error to managing the consequences of that error.

5. Faults Can Cross ECU Boundaries

Modern embedded machines often contain multiple controllers that communicate with each other.

A simplified fault path might look like:

Sensor
  ↓
Fault Detection
  ↓
Control Logic
  ↓
CAN / J1939
  ↓
Other ECU
  ↓
Machine Function

Now the fault-handling problem becomes larger.

The system may need to verify that:

  • The fault information is generated correctly.
  • The communication data represents the correct state.
  • The receiving ECU interprets the information correctly.
  • Message loss or timeout is handled correctly.
  • The machine enters the intended operating condition.

A fault that starts as a sensor problem can therefore become a communication and machine-behavior problem.

6. Recovery Deserves the Same Attention as Detection

One area that is easy to overlook is recovery.

Suppose a sensor becomes invalid and the software enters a fault state. A few cycles later, the sensor returns to a valid value.

Should the system immediately return to normal?

Not necessarily.

Depending on the requirements, the software may need to verify that the signal remains stable for a defined period or that other recovery conditions have been satisfied.

This helps prevent a system from repeatedly switching between normal and fault states because of a temporary or unstable signal.

7. Test the Fault as a Sequence, Not Just an Input

A unit test might verify individual input values:

Valid
Invalid
Maximum
Minimum

That is useful, but fault handling often depends on the sequence of events.

For example:

Valid
Valid
Invalid
Invalid
Invalid
Valid
Valid

represents a very different scenario from:

Valid
Invalid
Valid
Invalid
Valid

The first may represent a persistent fault, while the second may represent intermittent behavior.

Therefore, good fault-handling tests should consider:

  • Boundary inputs
  • Transient faults
  • Persistent faults
  • Repeated faults
  • Communication loss
  • Recovery conditions
  • Unexpected state transitions

8. Think Beyond the Individual Function

Unit testing is valuable because it verifies individual software components in isolation.

But a machine does not operate one function at a time.

The complete behavior may involve:

Input
  ↓
Signal Processing
  ↓
Fault Detection
  ↓
State Transition
  ↓
Control Logic
  ↓
Communication
  ↓
Diagnostics
  ↓
Machine Behavior
  ↓
Recovery

A problem can therefore exist between modules even when the individual functions pass their own tests.

9. A Better Question for Fault Testing

Instead of asking only:

“Does the fault-detection function work?”

ask:

“What happens to the complete system after this fault is detected?”

That question naturally leads to broader and more useful test scenarios.

You start checking not only whether the fault is detected, but also whether the system:

  • Transitions to the correct state
  • Applies the intended fallback behavior
  • Communicates the correct diagnostic information
  • Handles affected machine functions correctly
  • Prevents unsafe recovery
  • Returns to normal operation under the correct conditions

Key Takeaway

Fault handling should not be treated as a single error condition inside a function.

It is a system behavior.

Reliable embedded software needs more than correct fault detection. The complete system must also define and verify the reaction, communication, diagnostics and recovery behavior.

For embedded systems controlling physical machines, the most important question is not simply:

“Can the software detect the fault?”

It is:

“When something goes wrong, does the complete system behave exactly as intended?”

That is where robust fault handling becomes good embedded engineering.
blogs.short_description: A fault is more than an error condition in code. Learn how embedded systems can detect faults, enter safe states, communicate diagnostics, and recover correctly across software and machine functions.

blogs.title: Is 100% Code Coverage Enough for Embedded Software?
blogs.content:
Is 100% code coverage enough to say that embedded software is well tested? Not necessarily. Coverage tells us which code ran; it does not tell us whether the important behaviors and failure conditions were tested.

Coverage measures execution, not test quality

Statement coverage answers a narrow question: did a test execute this line? Branch coverage asks whether both outcomes of a decision ran. These measures help reveal unexecuted code, but neither tells us whether the test used meaningful inputs, checked the right result, or represented a real failure condition.

For example, a test can call a sensor-conversion function with one typical value and assert that it returns a number. The line may be covered, but the test may say nothing about values just outside the valid range, a disconnected sensor, stale data, arithmetic overflow, or the state the controller should enter after a reading fails.

Coverage is therefore useful evidence about the suite, not a certificate that the software is safe or correct. A high number can coexist with weak assertions, unrealistic test data, untested interfaces, or requirements that were never translated into tests.

Start with requirements and failure questions

Before writing a test, identify the behavior the requirement expects and the ways that behavior could fail. Ask questions such as: What is the valid input range? What happens at each limit? Can this value be missing, delayed, corrupted, or inconsistent with another signal? How should the function report an error? What must the caller do next?

For an embedded input-processing function, a useful set of cases could include:

  • A nominal reading in the middle of the valid range.
  • Values exactly at the lower and upper limits.
  • Values just below or above those limits.
  • Invalid encodings, sentinel values, or impossible combinations.
  • A timeout, stale sample, or unavailable hardware interface.
  • Recovery after the fault clears, including any required state reset.
  • Repeated faults and transitions between normal and fault states.

The expected result should be explicit for each case. It may be a returned value, an error code, a state transition, a diagnostic event, or a guarantee that an output remains in a defined safe state. A test that only executes code without checking the intended outcome adds little confidence.

Use coverage to find questions, not to chase a target

When a report shows an uncovered branch, investigate why. It may point to a missing test, a defensive path that needs a clear requirement, or dead code that should be removed. When coverage rises, review what the new tests actually assert. The goal is not simply to make a report greener; it is to understand what evidence the tests provide.

Coverage also has limits as a measure of behavior. A condition can be evaluated both ways without testing the combinations that matter. For higher-risk logic, teams may use stronger criteria such as condition/decision coverage or MC/DC when required by their process or standard. Those metrics still need sound requirements, representative tests, and engineering review; choosing a stricter metric does not make those activities unnecessary.

Test at the levels where failures appear

Unit tests are valuable for deterministic logic: conversions, state machines, range checks, protocol parsing, and error handling. They should be complemented by integration tests that exercise module boundaries and interfaces, then system or hardware-in-the-loop checks for timing, peripheral behavior, communication faults, and interactions with the surrounding machine.

A useful cycle is: requirement review, risk and failure analysis, test-case design, unit tests, coverage review, failure investigation, test or code rework, and integration and system validation. Findings at a later level should feed back into earlier tests. A bus timeout found on the bench, for instance, may reveal a missing unit-level recovery case as well as an integration test that needs to be kept.

Embedded context changes what matters

Embedded software does not run in isolation. A small decision can affect communication, sensors, actuators, timing, machine behavior, or another connected controller. Tests should consider stale or noisy signals, timeouts, reset behavior, resource limits, and the effect of faults on neighboring components—not only whether an individual function executes.

This does not mean every function needs an enormous test matrix. Prioritize based on the requirement, system impact, complexity, change history, and the consequences of failure. Make the reasoning visible so the team can understand what was tested and why.

A practical way to think about it

Code coverage helps answer, “Which parts of this code did our tests execute?” Good test design also asks, “Did we challenge the assumptions, verify the required outcomes, and exercise the failure and recovery behaviors that matter?” Both questions are useful, but the second is what turns a coverage report into engineering confidence.

I see code coverage as a measurement—not the definition of good testing. The real question is: Have we tested the behaviors and conditions that actually matter?

Read the original LinkedIn post.
blogs.short_description: Why high code coverage is only a measurement—and how boundary cases, invalid inputs, error handling, and system behavior make embedded tests stronger.

blogs.title: My Journey in Embedded Systems
blogs.content:
When I started working on off-highway construction machinery, I assumed the hard part would be the code. It wasn't. The hard part was everything around the code.

A Paver or a Compactor has to move several tonnes of asphalt while an operator sits several metres away holding a joystick. Embedded software on these machines is safety-relevant, and that single fact changes how you write it, how you test it, and how carefully you are allowed to change it six months later.

Start with the machine, not the datasheet

My early academic projects were Arduino sketches. You flash them over USB, they run, they do a thing. Commercial machinery firmware is different in one important way: you cannot simply reflash it. There is a machine sitting on a customer site that has to keep working, and a very expensive window in which it does not.

That constraint pushes you toward good habits early. Defensive checks on every input. Defaults that fail safe rather than fail fast. A boot path that leaves the machine in a defined state even if the application crashes halfway through initialisation.

Hardware teaches you what software cannot

Most of what I know about CAN, sensor behaviour and signal conditioning, I learned from hardware that did not behave the way the datasheet implied. A sensor that needs a settling time nobody documented. A connector that works perfectly on the bench and behaves differently when the machine vibrates. Pull-ups that are correct on paper and marginal in a hot enclosure next to a motor drive.

Software engineers are often told that the hardware is given. On machines, the hardware is a conversation partner, and you have to learn to hear it.

Tests are the part people underestimate

The part of my work I would emphasise to anyone starting out is unit testing. Using CANTATA across dozens of modules taught me more about my own code than writing it did. Coverage is a blunt metric, but the discipline behind it is not: if a branch is not exercised, nobody knows whether it works or merely appears to.

What I would tell my past self

  • Learn the protocol on a bench before you meet it on a machine.
  • Log generously. You will not be there when it breaks.
  • Write the failure path first, because it is the path that gets tested on a real machine.
  • Keep a steady Arduino or target board on your desk. Curiosity is cheapest when it is hardware.

The move from hobby boards to production firmware was less about learning a new language and more about learning a new standard of care. That part has stuck with me.
blogs.short_description: How I moved from Arduino boards to safety-relevant firmware on off-highway machinery, and what surprised me on the way.

blogs.title: CAN Protocol Best Practices
blogs.content:
CAN is a bus you can learn in an afternoon and still be getting wrong five years later. Most of what I have internalised came from sitting with a trace open in PCAN-Explorer while a machine refused to do what the code clearly said it should.

Identifier choice is a design decision

The 11-bit identifier field is only 11 bits, so something has to give. The usual compromise is to spend the low bits on the signal index and the high bits on the originating ECU. It is not elegant, but it means a decoder can filter on one or the other.

Whatever scheme you pick, write it down and keep it stable. A signal that moves address between firmware versions will break every tool, every test bench and every diagnostic routine you have.

Never trust the DLC you were told

It is tempting to assume the received length matches what you configured for transmission. It will not always be true, especially with gateway frames, diagnostic tools, or a device that has been reflashed with a mismatched database.

if (rx_dlc < expected_len) {
    /* Frame is short - discard, do not read past the buffer */
    return;
}
for (uint8_t i = 0; i < rx_dlc; i++) { ... }

Reading past the end of a received frame is one of the classic embedded C memory bugs, and the CAN peripheral will happily let you do it.

Filter aggressively

On a busy machine the bus carries far more traffic than your module cares about. Accepting every frame means waking your CPU for messages you will immediately discard. Configure the hardware acceptance filters so the MCU only sees what it needs.

This is both a CPU optimisation and a correctness one: the less unrelated traffic in your receive buffer, the less chance of processing a stale frame after a context switch.

Timeouts are part of the protocol

A signal that must arrive every 100 ms needs a timeout at around 300 ms. Without one, a disconnected sensor leaves your last-known value sitting in a variable indefinitely, and downstream logic treats stale data as current. Mark data invalid when it ages out, and make consumers check.

Debugging habits that pay off

  • Record raw traces with timestamps. Replaying a failure from a log beats guessing.
  • Watch the error frame counters. A climbing passive error counter explains a lot that a single dropped frame never will.
  • Check termination before you question the firmware. It is embarrassing and it is common.
  • Suspect the physical layer before the software layer. Signal integrity problems imitate logic bugs remarkably well.

None of this is exotic. It is the set of checks that stops a debugging session from turning into an afternoon of reading code that was never the problem.
blogs.short_description: Practical habits for implementing and debugging CAN in embedded C, learned from reading traces on real machines with PCAN-Explorer.

blogs.title: Real-time Debugging Techniques
blogs.content:
Console logging is wonderful right up until the moment you need to know what happened two hundred milliseconds ago on hardware that is already running a control loop. On machinery firmware you rarely get that luxury, so the approach has to be different.

Use the tools you actually have

My default stack is a hardware debugger for stepping and inspection, a CAN trace for what the machine is actually saying on the bus, and a GPIO or LED line for cheap timing evidence. The third one is underrated. Toggling a pin is a timing channel that costs you nothing and tells you exactly how long something took.

/* Measure how long the acquisition loop really takes */
GPIO_Set(DEBUG_PIN);
acquire_all_channels();
GPIO_Clear(DEBUG_PIN);   /* scope this - it is your period time */

Instrument for the failure you expect

Adding a counter to an error branch costs almost nothing and turns a vague symptom into a specific one. When a client reports that the machine 'sometimes does not start', a persisted fault counter read over CAN at the next opportunity answers the question immediately.

  • Keep a ring buffer in RAM of recent events, and dump it on demand rather than logging continuously.
  • Persist a reset cause and the events immediately before the reset. Post-mortem beats speculation.
  • Give every state machine an entry counter. If it never entered the fault state, the fault is elsewhere.

Reproduce before you theorise

The single biggest improvement to my debugging has been insisting on a reproducible trigger before I read a single line of the suspect module. A benchmark harness that drives the input interface directly, a loopback test, a fault-injection flag that forces the error condition on demand.

Once you can trigger a failure in under a minute, the difference between finding it and guessing about it becomes enormous.

Know what the hardware does under stress

Intermittent faults that only appear on a machine are often not firmware at all. Brown-outs, marginal regulators under motor load, EMI coupling into sensor lines, connectors that only fail when vibration is present. A scope on the suspect rail during a failure will find things no amount of source review will.

The summary

Debug with whatever evidence the system can give you, make failures reproducible, instrument the paths you care about ahead of time, and be willing to blame the hardware. Firmware is usually the last place to look, not the first.
blogs.short_description: How I debug firmware when there is no printf, the timing budget is tight, and the failure only happens on the machine.

blogs.title: An Introduction to J1939 Protocol
blogs.content:
J1939 is not a replacement for CAN. It is a set of conventions layered on top of it that standardise how heavy equipment identifies nodes, names parameters, and negotiates requests on the bus. Once you understand that framing, most of the specification stops being mysterious.

It is still CAN underneath

Every J1939 frame is a normal 29-bit extended identifier CAN frame. When you look at a trace, you see PGNs, source and destination addresses packed into the identifier field. J1939 defines how to interpret those bits; the CAN controller does the rest.

The identifier field

The 29-bit identifier carries priority, the PGN (Parameter Group Number), a source address, and for peer-to-peer messages a destination address. This is the detail that causes the most confusion: not every message carries a destination address.

Broadcast and destination-specific messages differ by PDU format, which is part of the PGN. Destination-specific frames include a target address; broadcast frames leave that field available for other purposes. Getting this backwards is a common cause of a module that appears to ignore perfectly valid requests.

Transport protocol for large payloads

A single CAN frame carries at most eight bytes, which is rarely enough for a block of diagnostic data. J1939 solves this with the transport protocol, where a large message is split into a connection-management phase and a series of data transfer frames, with the receiver acknowledging progress.

If a large transfer hangs partway, the place to look is almost always the connection management and abort behaviour rather than the payload itself.

Address claiming is the part that surprises people

On a J1939 network, a node does not simply have an address. It announces the address it intends to use, and if another node already claims it, one of them has to move or go offline. This means the address a module boots with is not necessarily the address it ends up with.

Consequences follow from this. Never assume your configured address is your active address. Read the negotiated address rather than caching it at startup.

Practical advice

  • Agree a PGN assignment with the other vendors before writing the code, not after.
  • Implement the address-claim state machine properly, including going offline if you lose the claim.
  • Decide byte order deliberately. Engineers assume big-endian with surprising frequency, and a mix-up is silent.
  • Handle unknown PGNs gracefully. Networks grow.

J1939 rewards the effort of reading the specification end to end once. It is dense, but almost all of its apparent complexity comes from a handful of conventions applied consistently.
blogs.short_description: A practical overview of the J1939 transport and addressing model, and why it sits on top of CAN rather than replacing it.

blogs.title: Optimizing Embedded Software Performance
blogs.content:
Performance work on embedded targets has an unfortunate reputation, and it deserves it. Hours spent shaving cycles out of a function that runs twice a second, while a blocking delay sits in a loop untouched by the whole exercise. Measure first, or do not bother.

Find out where the time actually goes

Before changing anything, establish a baseline and a profile. A GPIO toggle and a scope or logic analyser will tell you the real cost of a function. A cycle counter, where the hardware provides one, is better. Guessing at hot spots is the most common way to spend a day productively-looking and achieving nothing.

Where the time usually goes

In my experience the expensive things are rarely the arithmetic. They are:

  • Blocking waits. A busy-wait on a peripheral flag is the most common avoidable cost in firmware. Use the sleep mode, or restructure so the work happens elsewhere.
  • Unnecessary copying. Passing large structures by value through a call chain, or memcpy-ing a buffer that could have been processed in place.
  • Division and floating point. On targets without hardware support these can cost hundreds of cycles. Fixed-point arithmetic or a shift for powers of two usually does the job.
  • Repeated recalculation. A trigonometric call inside a per-sample loop where the value changes once per cycle.

Changes that reliably help

Make the common path cheap and the error path thorough. Branch prediction is weak on these cores, so put the likely case first and fall through.

Hoist invariants. Values that do not change inside a loop should not be recomputed inside it. Compilers catch some of this; they cannot catch all of it, especially across function calls.

Use the right integer widths. Moving from 32-bit arithmetic to 16-bit on an 8-bit core is one of the largest single wins available, because it is a change in the number of instructions, not in how clever the code looks.

/* Slow: recomputes the divisor scaling every sample */
uint32_t scale = 1000000u / rate_hz;
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    acc += (uint32_t)raw[i] * scale;
}

/* Better: rate_hz does not change within a cycle */
const uint32_t scale = 1000000u / rate_hz;
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    acc += (uint32_t)raw[i] * scale;
}

What not to do

  • Do not micro-optimise before the code is correct and tested. You will preserve the bugs and lose the structure.
  • Do not sacrifice readability for speed you have not measured.
  • Do not trade away the error handling to save cycles. A fast wrong answer on a machine is worse than a slow right one.

Stop when the timing budget is met. Optimisation past that point is effort with no return, and it usually shows up later as the reason nobody can change the code safely.
blogs.short_description: Measuring before optimising, and the small set of changes that usually deliver most of the gain on resource-constrained targets.
